The move took place on Saturday the fourteenth of February, on a cold, clear day when the sun sparkled on the snow on Kastanienallee. The Holzmann firm really had finished on the tenth, one day ahead of its own deadline, and on the eleventh a tradesman had come with a bunch of flowers, “with the compliments of the management”. The new bathroom had no step at all, it had a wide shower and two grab rails instead of one. Ludwig had tried them both and declared that he now felt as if he were in a luxury hotel.

At nine in the morning the whole house was on the stairs. Jakob and Andrei carried the heavy things: the wardrobe, the bed, the boxes of Ingrid's books, forty-two of them, Lena had counted. Kuba and Ola carried the light things and argued about who was allowed to carry the lamp. Mara stood at the bottom and gave directions as if she were on her ward at the hospital. Mrs Nowak from the second floor brought coffee in a huge Thermos. And Fritz lay on the landing and watched them all, with the weary look of a dog who has seen many removals and never found one any good.

The hardest part was Ingrid's armchair. It was old and heavy and barely fitted through the door, and Ludwig insisted that nobody was allowed to tilt it. “On the one hand,” said Jakob, panting, halfway up the stairs, “I understand. On the other hand, it would be down in two minutes if we were allowed to put it on its side.” “Admittedly you're right,” Ludwig answered from below, “but my wife read in this armchair for twenty-five years. It stays upright.” It took twenty minutes. When the armchair finally stood at the window overlooking the courtyard, next to the tiled stove, the whole staircase applauded.

After that there was a break with coffee and Andrei's apple cake, on removal boxes in the courtyard, in the cold winter sun. Kuba wanted to know why Ludwig was actually moving if he loved the old flat so much. “That's a good question,” said Ludwig. “On the one hand I love it. On the other hand I also love my knee, and my knee has made a complaint. Formally. With a deadline.” Kuba laughed, but Ola, who was always more serious than her brother, asked: “And are you sad?” Ludwig thought about it. “Admittedly I'm a little sad,” he said, “but mostly I'm curious. At eighty-three you're not often curious any more. You have to make the most of it.”

At twelve o'clock someone rang the bell at the front door. Lena opened it. Outside stood a woman of fifty-seven, of medium height, with short grey hair, a red woolly hat and a small suitcase. She looked at Lena, then past her into the stairwell, at the letterboxes, at the old floor tiles, at the banister. And then she said, very quietly, more to herself than to Lena: “The tiles. You still have the same tiles. With the little crack next to the door. I made it. With my scooter. In 1983.”

Ludwig came out of his new flat, leaning on his stick. He and Susanne looked at each other for a long time without saying anything. They had never seen each other. But they knew each other through a tin box, a blue school exercise book, a class photo from 1981 and three letters. Then Ludwig said: “You've cut off your plaits.” And Susanne laughed and cried at the same time, and then they hugged, an old man and a teacher from Hanover, in the middle of the stairwell, among removal boxes, while Fritz wagged his tail for the first time that day.

In the afternoon, when most of the boxes were unpacked, Susanne sat in Ingrid's armchair by the window. Ludwig had insisted. She held the tin box on her knees and the blue exercise book in her hand and read from it aloud, in her teacher's voice, for everyone who could fit into the little flat: Lena and Andrei on the floor, Mara and Jakob on the windowsill, Kuba and Ola on the rug, Michael, who had come specially from Munich, in the doorway. She read about a little girl who couldn't read and about a teacher who came every Wednesday and never gave up. She read about a boy from the first floor who played the guitar badly. She read about the ninth of November.

At one point she stopped. It was a page from March 1982, with big, unsteady letters, and underneath, in red ink, a sentence in different handwriting. Susanne handed the exercise book to Ludwig. He recognised the handwriting at once. “Today you read a whole page by yourself for the first time. I am very proud of you. Mrs Brandt.” Ludwig ran his finger over the red letters, very carefully, as if they might disappear. They were fifty years old. The room was so quiet that you could hear the tiled stove crackling.

I have to confess something to you. I wasn't sure whether I should come. I weighed it up for three nights. On the one hand I wanted to see the flat, on the other hand I was afraid. Afraid that the memory would be spoilt if I compared it with reality. My husband said: admittedly it may hurt, but if you don't go, you'll regret it all your life. He was right. He's almost always right. It's very tiring.

Michael, who was standing in the doorway, cleared his throat. “Can I say something too? I have some news. Not completely certain, but nearly. A colleague of mine knows a music teacher in Leipzig, and he knows a guitarist who lived in Prenzlauer Berg in the eighties. Today he plays in an orchestra, in Dresden. His name is Mirko.” Susanne went pale. Nobody said anything. “I haven't called him yet,” Michael added quickly. “I thought you should decide that. What speaks in favour is that you'd finally know. What speaks against it…” “Nothing speaks against it,” said Susanne quietly. “Only my fear. And I already had that once today, and it was wrong.”

Everyone laughed. Then Susanne put the exercise book back in the box and looked round the room, slowly, as if she wanted to fix every detail in her mind: the tiled stove, the window overlooking the courtyard, the old chestnut tree outside, the armchair, the forty-two boxes of books. “The memory hasn't been spoilt,” she said. “On the contrary. Now it isn't just my flat any more. Now it's yours. Yours, I mean, Ludwig. And Mrs Brandt's. She was always here, back then too, every Wednesday. Now she lives here again.”

In the evening, when Susanne was asleep in the guest room at Mara's and all the others had gone, Ludwig sat alone in his new flat. It was quiet. Above him, on the first floor, he could hear footsteps: Lena and Andrei, already carrying the first boxes into his old flat, laughing, arguing about where the bed should go. He heard Lena say: “Admittedly the bedroom is bigger, but the light is nicer in the living room.” And Andrei: “On the one hand you're right, on the other hand I don't want to sleep in the living room.” Ludwig smiled. They were learning fast, both of them. Not just German. Arguing too, the lovely, loving kind of arguing you can only have with someone you don't want to lose.

Later someone knocked softly at his door. It was Susanne, in her coat, with her phone in her hand. “I couldn't sleep,” she said. “I asked Michael to give me the number. I'll call tomorrow. Not today. Today has been enough. But tomorrow.” Ludwig nodded. “Tomorrow is a good day for phone calls,” he said. “I didn't call Ingrid till the day after our first meeting either. She said I'd waited too long. A whole day!” Susanne laughed and went back upstairs, and Ludwig heard her footsteps on the stairs, light and quick, like those of a little girl with plaits.

He stood up, went to the tiled stove and put his hand on the warm green tiles. “Well, Ingrid,” he said quietly. “To sum up, you can say: it was a good day.” Outside, in the courtyard, the light from Lena's new window fell on the snow, a warm yellow square, exactly where the light from his window had once fallen. The house, he thought, had only swapped floors. The heart had stayed.
